newsitem.title: POLAND: Walesa lauds fellow Polish Nobel laureate.
newsitem.headline: Walesa lauds fellow Polish Nobel laureate.

text.p: Polish ex-president Lech Walesa lauded poet Wislawa Szymborska on Thursday as a modest person with a great heart and pen, just hours after the announcement that his compatriot had won the 1996 Nobel prize for literature.
Walesa, himself a winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, said of the shy and retiring Szymborska: "I am especially proud of this Nobel prize as Poland has again been recognised."

"In particular a woman has been recognised, who is so modest as a person and so great of heart and pen," Walesa told reporters at his office in Solidarity union headquarters in the Baltic city of Gdansk.
Walesa gained his own prize in 1983, when he was the interned leader of the union during its peaceful struggle for democracy, which ended with the 1989 downfall of communism.
He said he had heard of Thursday's decision by the Swedish academy with possibly greater emotion than when he learned of his own distinction.

Another Polish-born Nobel winner, poet Czeslaw Milosz who was honoured in 1980, hailed the decision in a radio interview from the United States where he lives, as "a great triumph of Polish 20th century poetry".
President Aleksander Kwasniewski, who unseated Walesa in elections last year, wrote to tell Szymborska that her triumph was above all her own.
"There is no doubt that it is also a great achievement of Polish literature," wrote Kwasniewski, thanking the 73-year-old for adding so notably to Poland's fame.
Szymborska's prize takes to five the number of Poles or Polish-born writers to take the Nobel literature award.
Novelist Henryk Sienkiewicz won in 1905 for his book on early Christian suffering "Quo Vadis", and Wladyslaw Reymont in 1924 for his forceful novel of rural life "The Peasants".
Polish-born Jewish novelist Isaac Bashevis Singer won the prize in 1978 and Czeslaw Milosz in 1980, although both by then had become American citizens.
In addition to them, and to Walesa's 1983 peace prize, the country was honoured by two science prizes awarded to Marie Curie-Sklodowska, the Polish-born pioneer in the field of radiation.
In 1903 she shared a physics prize with her French husband, then in 1911 won a chemistry prize for discovering two new elements.
